opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think coding took off first because it has a property most domains don't: you can verify the output. Code compiles or it doesn't, tests pass or they fail, and that tight feedback loop makes it a great fit for these models. So when I think about what's next, I look for domains that share some of that structure, or where we can build it.

Science is the one I'm most excited about, especially the life sciences. There's a huge amount of data in biology, in genomics, protein structure, and cell imaging, and we're building models that are superhuman at prediction in some of these areas. But a model that predicts well isn't the same as a model that teaches us something. If a model can tell you which protein will fold a certain way, or which patients will respond to a treatment, the real value is in understanding *why*. That's where I think the next big wave comes from: not just using models as black-box oracles, but opening them up and pulling out the knowledge they've learned. Those models may have found real biology that no human has articulated yet.

That's also why I spend so much time on interpretability. As these systems move from writing code to high-stakes domains like medicine, finance, and scientific discovery, "trust me, it works" stops being good enough. You need to understand what the model is doing, debug it when it fails, and steer it precisely. Coding let us get away with less of that because you can just run the code. In science and medicine, the cost of being wrong is much higher and the ground truth is slower to come by.

So my short answer is scientific discovery, but with an asterisk. The applications that win won't just generate outputs. They'll be built on models we actually understand, where we can extract new insights and have confidence in what they're telling us.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that coding was the easy case, and that's worth understanding before predicting what's next. Code has a tight feedback loop: you can run it, test it, see if it compiles, and the model gets a signal almost immediately. The data is abundant and public, and the people building the tools are also the users, so iteration is incredibly fast.

So the question I ask is: where else do you get something close to that loop? My answer is biology, and specifically the wet-lab side of drug discovery and protein engineering. It doesn't look like coding on the surface, because an experiment takes days or weeks rather than milliseconds. But structurally it's similar. You have a hypothesis, you have a verifiable outcome, and you have a lot of latent structure in the data that humans have never been able to fully exploit. Every protein sequence is, in a sense, a program that nature wrote, and we now have models that can read and increasingly write in that language.

What changed in the last couple of years is that the experimental side started catching up. Automated labs and cheaper sequencing mean you can actually close the loop. A model proposes a hundred candidates, the lab tests them, the results come back, and the model updates. That's the same shape as an agent writing code and running tests. It's just slower and more expensive per iteration, which is why it comes second rather than first.

The part I'd flag for people building in this space is that the winners won't be the ones with the best model in isolation. They'll be the ones who own the loop, meaning the data generation, the experimental infrastructure, and the ability to learn from every failed experiment rather than just the successful ones. Most of the value in biology sits in negative results that nobody publishes. Whoever accumulates that becomes very hard to catch.

If I had to name a dark horse beyond biology, I'd say materials and chemistry for the same reason. Same loop, same opportunity, slightly less attention right now.

astra-6.text:
My guess is that the next major impact will be in knowledge work where the task is less neatly defined than coding. Think about operations: gathering information from different systems, figuring out what needs to happen, and following through.

Coding has a powerful feedback loop—you can run the code and see whether it works. In other domains, success is harder to measure, and that makes reliability harder. So I’d look for workflows where the outcome is clear and a person can review the important decisions. Customer support is one example; parts of finance and administrative work are others.

The big shift is when AI can move from giving you a useful answer to completing a useful piece of work. I think that’s where we’ll see a lot of the next wave of value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next big impact will be in work where there’s a lot of information to synthesize and a fairly clear way to check the result. Coding has that feedback loop: you can run the code and see whether it works. The interesting question is where we can build similar feedback loops in other fields.

Customer support and operations are good candidates. There’s a big difference between an AI that answers a question about a refund and one that can actually resolve the issue. That means understanding the context, using the right systems, and knowing when to bring in a person. I think moving from generating an answer to completing that whole workflow is where we’ll see a lot of value.
